title: Did Early Humans Keep Souvenirs 500,000 Years Ago?
paragraphs: Souvenirs seem quintessentially modern, a by-product of travel and sentiment. A paper in Evolutionary Anthropology nonetheless proposes that the impulse to hoard tokens of experience is far older, taking shape perhaps half a million years ago among hominins living in what is now Israel.

The argument draws on three strands of evidence. Colourful pebbles at Qesem Cave were ferried in from elsewhere and appear to have had no practical function; weathered flint tools were retained with their ancient surfaces largely untouched; and in the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were knapped so that fossils or odd geological formations remained at the heart of the stone. The authors, from Tel Aviv and Oxford, read these as external memory devices: tangible anchors that could summon a place or an episode, help owners tell first-hand experience from hearsay and lend weight to personal testimony, thereby smoothing cooperation. Ran Barkai adds that the waning of large animals such as elephants may have pushed groups into unfamiliar hunting grounds, making reminders of those places worth keeping.

Yet the paper is candid about its limits. It is a hypothesis, not a proof, and a stone cannot testify to its own significance. Whether such behaviour truly nudged the evolution of autobiographical memory will depend on whether further discoveries echo the pattern rather than on the charm of the narrative.

questions.q: What three kinds of evidence does the argument rely on?
questions.a: Colourful pebbles at Qesem Cave, retained weathered flint tools, and handaxes built around fossils in the Sakhnin Valley.

questions.q: How might keepsakes have helped social life?
questions.a: They could help owners separate first-hand experience from hearsay and lend weight to personal accounts, supporting cooperation.

questions.q: Why does the article say the narrative alone is not enough?
questions.a: Because the idea is a hypothesis and a stone cannot show its own meaning; further discoveries are needed.
